Analyze how changes in turnout across demographic and geographic groups in Wisconsin from 2016 to 2020 relate to shifts in vote share for the presidential and House races: compute correlations or regression estimates linking turnout change by county/precinct (and by demographic groups such as age, race/ethnicity, education, and urban/suburban/rural classification) to changes in party vote share, and identify which turnout changes (e.g., higher youth turnout, increased Black turnout, suburban turnout shifts) most strongly associate with gains or losses for each party.

Give the official, certified 2020 Wisconsin presidential election results: statewide totals for each candidate, statewide vote percentages, the statewide margin of victory, and the certified county-level vote totals and percentages for the top presidential candidates (showing margins in each county).

For each Wisconsin congressional district in 2020, compare the U.S. House general election margin (winner minus runner-up in votes and percentage) to the presidential general election margin within that same district (using precinct-to-district apportionment or county-level returns mapped to the district), and report which races were more Democratic or more Republican relative to the other race.

Identify the specific Wisconsin statutes, administrative rules, and emergency orders (state executive or WEC guidance) that governed absentee and mail-in voting for the November 3, 2020 general election. Include concrete procedural details: application and ballot request deadlines, the last date a ballot could be postmarked vs received and still count, witness/attestation and photo ID requirements or any temporary waivers, use and regulation of ballot drop boxes, signature verification standards, and any county-level variations or clerk memoranda that changed routine practice in 2020 (cite section numbers, order names/dates, or specific clerk directives).
sub_answers.text: Mail-in ballots were more likely to have errors than in-person ballots, and about 560,000 U.S. mail ballots (about 1%) were rejected in 2020 for identity verification errors, resulting in those votes not being counted [d78408403s1p0]. CISA recommended tiered steps for reviewing signatures beginning with software-based systems, then human inspection, and ending with a bipartisan review team making a final determination of signature validity [d78408403s1p0]. Two-thirds of states require election officials to notify voters of a missing signature or signature discrepancy and to give voters an opportunity to correct it, with notification methods and deadlines specified by each state [d78408403s3p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Describe the end-to-end processing and counting workflow for Wisconsin ballots in the 2020 general election, with separate, specific steps for: in-person voting (poll book check-in, provisional ballots), absentee/mail ballots (receipt handling, envelope chain-of-custody logs, signature comparison, curing procedures), central count vs polling place tabulation (machine models used, software/firmware, how optical scan adjudication was handled), provisional ballot adjudication and acceptance criteria, canvass meeting procedures at the municipal and county level (who signs what and when), observer/party access rules, and how overvotes/undervotes and adjudicated ballots were documented in logs and reports (cite forms or log names where possible).
sub_answers.text: Ballots were routinely challenged for incomplete ID information, missing or mismatched signatures, or lacking required witness signatures, with causes including changes in voter signatures over time, outdated IDs, or name changes [d78408403s2p0]. Correction processes varied by jurisdiction and could include submitting an affidavit with ID, sending a form or a whole new ballot, and some jurisdictions would spoil and reissue a ballot when a required witness signature was missing [d78408403s4p0]. When mail-in ballots were flagged for curing, jurisdictions followed notification procedures to contact voters and offer an opportunity to fix the issue, and non-governmental organizations sometimes contacted challenged voters as well [d78408403s3p0]. A notable portion of flagged mail-in ballots were successfully cured in practice; for example, two thirds of Nevada’s 17,734 flagged mail-in ballots in 2022 were successfully cured and counted, demonstrating curing can change final counts when applied [d78408403s4p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List the statutory and administrative mechanisms for post-election review in Wisconsin applicable to federal elections in 2020, and explain how they were executed: thresholds and procedures for automatic and candidate-requested recounts, the step-by-step recount process used in 2020 (who conducted counts, how ballots were inspected and re-tabulated, timelines and deadlines), whether Wisconsin used any post-election audits or risk-limiting audits in 2020 and how they were run, the state certification timeline and authority (WEC or other body), roles of county clerks and the state in certifying results, any court orders or special procedures invoked in 2020, and public reporting or final findings from recounts/audits (include dates, case names, or docket numbers if applicable).
sub_answers.text: As of November 6, 2020, there was no evidence that ballot curing was being used to commit election fraud [d78408403s1p0]. Studies showed a measurable fraction of ballots were rejected but many challenged ballots could be cured and counted, with one study finding 60% of challenged signatures were fixed and counted prior to certification in Washington State analysis [d78408403s1p0]. Post-election litigation in 2020 included multiple suits seeking to restrict aspects of absentee voting and drop box use and challenging equipment, with courts dismissing some of those challenges in other states [d61627193s10p0]. Investigations in some states concluded no evidence of widespread voter fraud in 2020 elections, as in one state's concluding investigation in April 2021 [d63363293s25p0].
